newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan polls may not lead to political stability.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan polls may not lead to political stability.

text.p: Pakistanis go to the polls on Monday for the fourth time in nine years, but analysts say the election may not restore stability to their troubled nation as it celebrates its 50th anniversary of independence.
President Farooq Leghari called the polls after he sacked former ally Benazir Bhutto's three-year-old government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.

The main contest for control of the 217-seat National Assembly (lower house) and four provincial assemblies is between the two big parties -- the Pakistan Muslim League led by Nawaz Sharif and Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party.

But analysts doubt the next government will be able to halt a perennial power struggle between president and prime minister or reduce the political influence of the armed forces, which have ruled Pakistan for 24 years in the past half-century.
"The first question to ask is whether there is something that exists right now called Pakistani democracy," said Paula Newberg of Washington's Georgetown University in an interview.

"You have a constitution that is internally contradictory and includes within it significant anti-democratic elements, including the capacity somehow to set the government aside and yet to keep functioning," she said.

Pervez Hoodbhoy, a lecturer at Islamabad's Quaid-e-Azam University, told Reuters successive governments had failed to deliver on their promises, leading to the present crisis that was complicated by the role of the military.

"Today Pakistan is ruled by a coterie of feudal families. Its policies and its priorities are dictated by the military," he said. "This is an intolerable situation. It is driving this country to disintegration and disaster."
"The wrongs this country is suffering from, the failures in governance are inherent," said political analyst Aziz Sidiqui.
He said the continued interference of the military had stunted political parties and prevented them from maturing.
"The problems that have come up are because of these distortions in the form of martial law in Pakistan. This impatience with democratic government worsens the situation."

Asma Jehangir of the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan said the bane of political system was the tussle for power between the presidency and the premiership, which had tilted towards the former during the caretaker government.
"In the last few months, I have not seen many decisions being taken by the prime minister," she said. "It is very obvious that we are moving towards a presidential system."
Jehangir said Leghari's creation last month of a Council for Defence and National Security under his own chairmanship had further curtailed the powers of a prime minister.
The council, bringing together senior ministers and top generals, gives the military its first formal say in government.
Zafar Iqbal Cheema, a political science professor at Quaid-e-Azam University, said that public frustration with politicians had increased.
"People are inclined to think that frequent elections are no solution to the problems," he said. "The parties do not have leaderships capable of delivering what they have promised."
Pakistan, he argued, was gradually becoming ungovernable.
Cheema also pointed to the division of powers between the president and prime minister as the constitution's fatal flaw.

"You can't divide executive powers and give some of them to the president and some to the prime minister," he said. "Wherever there is a division of executive powers, they fight with each other, particularly when the responsibilites overlap.
"Unless you remove that inbuilt recipe for disaster, any individual in that place will fight with the other," he said.
